units: the writer sends news to a close acquaintance about a plot taken back in hand
a layer of plant matter has been spread over the ground to hold the moisture
the hedge has been filled out with pieces taken from shrubs
the plants kept in place put up with a lack of water
building rubble has to be carted off because it blocks water soaking in
the writer notices that rain is held better since the work was done
roots are reaching further down than they used to
the writer asks after the food crop of the person written to
text: Dear friend, here at last is the news you asked for about the plot we took back in hand behind the house. Three jobs have kept me busy, and I will run through them in order. The first was the ground itself: I spread a thick layer of dead leaves over it, so that the damp stays put and less water lifts away. The second was the hedge, which I filled out with cuttings taken from the shrubs that stand up best to a dry spell. The third is the dreary one, carting off the heap of rubble the old shed left behind, since it stops the rain soaking in. Already the leaf layer holds a downpour better, and the roots are reaching further down than they used to. Small efforts of that sort will count for more than regret once the weather turns harsher still. Write soon, and tell me how your vegetable patch is faring.

units: a heavy fuel escaped from a store towards a watercourse
the leak went unnoticed through the first week
fishermen then saw weakened fish
a coloured film spread across the surface of the water
the technical authorities turned out only once the intake was threatened
floating devices were put in to hold back the slick
the fouled sediment was scraped away after the pumping
wildlife is coming back to the site little by little
a smell lingers on the bank in strong heat
text: So you want to know what became of the river after the trouble at the fuel store? Here it is in order. For the first week nobody noticed a thing: the heavy oil was seeping out under a cracked slab, giving off nothing you could smell from the bank. Then the fishermen started pulling up listless fish, and a coloured film crept across the still water. Was anything done quickly, you ask? Not at all, and that is the part which still rankles. Only when the slick reached the drinking water intake did the technical crew turn out. After that it moved along. Floating booms went in, the oily layer was pumped off, and the fouled silt was scraped away. And now? Now the wildlife is edging back, though the bank still gives off a tarry smell whenever the heat builds. That is roughly where matters stand today, as far as anyone can tell.

units: the spring feeding an upper district is running dry
draws made for crops have emptied the underground store
a grower fears losing his harvest without watering
a teacher asks the official about supply brought in by lorry
the official accepts that this would become necessary the following summer
the council means to cap the volumes allowed
the leaking pipes will be mended
the watering of ornamental ground will be banned
the public accepts that its own uses add to the shortage
text: The head of the water service put it bluntly to the residents gathered in the lower hall: the spring feeding the upper district is running dry. Pumping for crops, she explained, had emptied the underground store through the dry months, and one thing was now dragging another after it. A grower answered that his fields would burn without watering. A teacher asked whether the children would end up drinking water brought in by lorry. The official accepted that it would come to that by the following summer if nothing changed. The council, she added, would cap the volumes allowed, mend the leaking pipes and ban the watering of lawns. The talk ran on well into the evening, with everyone taking the point that the shortage was not the fault of the sky alone, but of what every household draws.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: the channel of a harbour was silting up season after season
ships could no longer reach the quays
the merchants wrongly believed that the sea was drawing back
the river was in fact bringing down mud torn from the slopes
the felling of trees had left the hillsides bare
engineers tied the ruin of the heights to the decline of the harbour
planting was ordered on the ridges
brushwood works were set in the gullies
basins were dug to trap the mud before the shore
the depth of the navigable passage was regained
text: A thriving harbour town once watched its channel silt up, season upon season. Ships laden with salt and timber scraped the bottom, then gave up the run up to the quays altogether. The merchants feared the sea was drawing back; in truth the river was tipping into the roadstead a load of mud torn from the slopes above. Tall stands of trees had been felled for roof beams, leaving the hillsides bare, and the rain carried the soil off with nothing to check it. In time a generation of engineers grasped what tied the stripped hill to the ailing port. They had the ridges replanted, brushwood hurdles woven along the gullies and basins dug where the mud would settle before ever reaching the shore. The channel found its depth again, and the lesson outlived by many years those who had first learned it.

units: two neighbouring roofs behave differently under the sun
the first carries a dark bituminous covering
this surface takes in nearly all the radiation reaching it
the heating spoils the insulation laid beneath
the cooling plant then runs without a break
the second joins a pale render to a cover of plants
this roof throws back part of the radiation and holds rainwater
the pale version stays cooler at the same hour of reading
the planted roof weighs more and calls for steady upkeep
text: Two roofs side by side behave in opposite ways under the sun, and the covering explains it. The first carries a dark bituminous sheet, close to tar, which takes in nearly all the sunlight reaching it. Its surface grows so hot that the insulation laid beneath ages early, and the cooling plant runs without a break. The second has a pale mineral render, topped with a mat of fleshy plants. It throws back a good share of the radiation and holds rainwater in its growing layer. Read at the same hour, the pale roof stays markedly cooler than the dark one. The gap shows up on the energy bill of the building as well. Against that, the planted roof weighs more and calls for steady upkeep, which the sheet never asks for. The choice turns as much on the frame below as on the weather.

units: the keeper of a high station tells of an episode from his last season of work
the packed snow was covered with a greyish deposit
this deposit came from fires burning far away
a darkened surface takes in more heat and melts faster
the buried instruments had to be dug out twice in the same week
the slope was oddly silent at night
the usual night-time flows had gone
the observer wrote down what he saw in a notebook
readings from later seasons bore out his impression
text: The keeper of a high station tells of an episode that stayed with him through his last season of readings. He speaks first of the colour of the packed snow: instead of the expected white, the surface wore a grey veil of soot laid down by fires burning far away. He turns next to the melting, quickened because a darkened surface takes in more heat. He describes the buried instruments, which had to be dug out twice in the same week as the mantle sank. He recalls, last of all, the odd hush on the slope, stripped of the meltwater streams that usually ran through the night. Back down at the hut he entered these remarks in a bound notebook, aware that a lone story of that kind proves nothing on its own. Readings from later seasons bore him out, and the pages of that notebook seeded a much wider study.

units: the roof must be looked over and clean before any collecting
a guard is fitted at the mouth of the gutter to hold back leaves
the tank is set on firm footing and out of the sun
a collector carrying a filter joins the downpipe to the tank
the overflow must run towards planted ground and not onto the road
the water of the first week serves to rinse and is then thrown away
the tightness of the lid is tested each season
an open vessel encourages mosquitoes to breed
the store is partly drawn down before the frost to avoid a split
text: Before you start collecting rainwater at home, look the roof over carefully: a clean covering, free of moss and grime, yields clearer water. Fit a guard at the mouth of the gutter, so that the leaves are held back. Stand the tank on firm footing, out of the sun, so that warmth does not feed the algae. Join the downpipe to it with a collector carrying a filter, and check that the overflow can run into a bed of planting rather than out onto the road. Run the tap through the first week to rinse the tank, then throw that water away. Each season, test the lid for a tight seal, since an open vessel encourages mosquitoes to breed. Lastly, draw the store partly down before the frosts, or the ice will split the wall. Water gathered in this way will do for watering the garden and for cleaning tools.

units: an old coastal path has been shut off by a fence
the sea is hollowing out the foot of the rock wall
storm spells have grown more frequent
each assault carries off soft rock at the base of the slope
the upper part ends up giving way
a dwelling was pulled down over the previous cold season
its rubble still litters the beach lying below
a councillor explains that pulling back and staying both cost dear
scientists find the pace quickening with the rise of the sea
the parking areas are being shifted inland
text: Up on the cliff, the first thing you notice is the orange fencing shutting off the old coast path. The people living there will tell you straight away: the sea is hollowing out the foot of the wall, and the top follows. Since the storms started coming round more often, every swell carries off a little marl at the base of the slope, until the rock above gives way. So a house had to be pulled down over the cold season, and its rubble still litters the beach below. The councillor who handles the shoreline makes no secret of the bind: pulling back costs dear, staying put costs dearer. Scientists out measuring the retreat confirm that the pace is quickening as the sea rises. Meanwhile the parking areas are shifted inland, access is barred, warnings go up. And the fencing creeps further in each winter.

units: from a distance a wetland looks like an ordinary meadow
straight ditches were cut long ago to drain the marsh
this draining was meant to win ground for grazing
the water runs off towards a canal instead of staying in the hollows
peat left open to the air gives up its carbon
the birds that nested in the rushes have quit the site
wardens are plugging the ditches with clay
the water table is lifted and the reeds come back
boardwalks keep visitors clear of the frail ground
amphibians took to the pools from the second season
text: Seen from a distance along the towpath, the wetland looks like an ordinary meadow, grassy and cropped short. Closer to, straight ditches appear, cut long ago to drain the marsh and win grazing for stock. The water now slides off towards the canal instead of lingering in the hollows, and the bared peat gives up its carbon to the air. The birds that nested in the clumps of rush have quit the place. A team of wardens is working to turn that round: they plug the ditches with clay stoppers, lift the water table and let the reeds come back. Boardwalks steer walkers clear of the frail ground. By the second season the rewetted pools had taken in amphibians, and the sodden peat had stopped smouldering. The scene now looks a good deal less tidy, and that is exactly the sign they were waiting for.

units: the writer disputes the sporting image used to describe climate action
a contest is run alone and comes to an end at a set term
the writer offers the image of ground tended in common
each person there takes on the state of the soil left by the others
the careless gardener harms the plot next door
changing the image changes the nature of the commitments expected
a promise of figures differs from a promise of continued upkeep
the writer calls for talk of care rather than of performance
later generations will judge what has survived
text: We are fond of casting the climate effort as a race, with its winners and its stragglers. The picture is appealing, and it leads us astray. A race is run alone and comes to an end; the climate is closer to a shared garden, where each of us takes on the soil the others have left behind. In a race, whoever slows loses ground; in a garden, whoever lets a plot go lets the weeds through to the plot beside it. The switch matters: it changes what we expect of the promises made. A runner pledges a score, a gardener pledges upkeep. One of them marks a finish, the other marks a going on. We would do better, then, to speak less of records and more of care, less of standings and more of seasons. Those who come after us will not ask who ran the hardest; they will look at what is still growing.
